newsitem.title: USA: Experts hit defense theory in Simpson civil trial.
newsitem.headline: Experts hit defense theory in Simpson civil trial.

text.p: Expert witnesses called by plaintiffs in O.J. Simpson's civil trial Thursday attacked the defence theory that blood was planted by police and the evidence was contaminated in a botched investigation.
One expert said it was "absolutely ridiculous" to suggest that evidence had been contaminated and a second said there was no evidence that blood had been planted in the case.
Although the preservative EDTA was present in trace amounts in blood evidence, molecular biologist Terry Lee said, that did not mean the blood had been planted.
Defence lawyers have claimed that blood from samples taken from Simpson and from the body of his ex-wife was planted by police to incriminate the former football star.

But Lee said the blood evidence from the crime scene and from Simpson's home, identified as that of Simpson and his murdered ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, contained EDTA in amounts that were so minute as to make it impossible for the blood to have come from the reference samples. EDTA is present in the test tubes used to store reference blood samples to ensure that the samples do not coagulate.

Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 of the June 12, 1994, murders of his ex-wife and and her friend Ronald Goldman and is now battling a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.

The chemical was found in blood from the back gate of Nicole Brown's condominium identified as Simpson's and on a sock found in Simpson's bedroom and identified as Nicole Brown Simpson's. EDTA is not present in the human body.

Lee, who reviewed the work of FBI scientist Roger Martz, who tested the blood for EDTA, said Martz first tested the references samples for EDTA in his chromotography machine before he ran the blood evidence through it. He said the EDTA detected in the blood evidence came from residue left in the machine. "It is a common problem with these instruments."
Lee added that the amount of EDTA found in the blood evidence was 100 times smaller than that found in the reference samples.

Another expert, molecular geneticist Brad Popovich, said he had reviewed all the Los Angeles Police Department evidence collection techniques in the case as well as the testing procedures at the LAPD crime laboratory and at two other laboratories involved and found no contamination. At one point in his testimony he said it was "absolutely ridiculous" for the defence to suggest that there was.

Popovich said there were three opportunities for contamination: during evidence collection, when it was being handled in the LAPD crime laboratory and when the blood evidence was undergoing DNA testing. He said an exhaustive review of all three procedures led him to believe there was "absolutely no contamination of evidence in this case."
